description_full: Danaher Corporation designs, manufactures, and markets professional, medical, research, and industrial products and services in the United States, China, and internationally. The company operates through Biotechnology, Life Sciences, and Diagnostics segments. The Biotechnology segment provides technologies, consumables, services, and solutions that advance, accelerate, and integrate the development and manufacture of therapeutics; cell line and cell culture media development services; cell culture media, process liquids and buffers for manufacturing, chromatography resins, filtration technologies, and aseptic fill finish; single-use hardware, consumables, and services, such as the design and installation of full manufacturing suites; lab filtration, separation, and purification; lab-scale protein purification and analytical tools; reagents, membranes, and services for diagnostic and assay development; and healthcare filtration solutions. The Life Sciences segment provides mass spectrometers; bioanalytical measurement systems; flow cytometry, genomics, lab automation, centrifugation, liquid handling automation instruments, antibodies and reagents, and particle counting and characterization; genome sample preparation; microscopes; protein consumables; filtration products; and genomic medicines, such as custom nucleic acid products, and plasmid DNA, RNA, and proteins under the ABCAM, ALDEVRON, BECKMAN COULTER, GENEDATA, IDT, LEICA MICROSYSTEMS, MOLECULAR DEVICES, PALL, PHENOMENEX, and SCIEX brands. The Diagnostics segment offers clinical instruments, consumables, software, and services that hospitals, physicians' offices, reference laboratories and other critical care settings use to diagnose disease and make treatment decisions. The company was formerly known as Diversified Mortgage Investors, Inc. and changed its name to Danaher Corporation in 1984. Danaher Corporation was incorporated in 1969 and is headquartered in Washington, the District Of Columbia.

financial_summary: Danaher Corporation is a large-cap healthcare business with a $161.9B market cap on $24.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 56% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $5.3B in free cash flow — roughly 21 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.78× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage of 18× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 11% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.2× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 19pp above the Healthcare median (0%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.17x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.5% of sector revenue and 1.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.05 across 458 companies in the universe; the top four hold 35% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 30% and a beta of 0.95, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.32 vs 5y 0.94), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $752.3M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 28% in the 2020 crash, 25% in the 2022 bear market and 45% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $183 (margin of safety -26%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 29%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $126 to $267 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Healthcare peers: P/E 38.1 vs 25.5, EV/EBITDA 22.0 vs 15.7 and P/FCF 30.8 vs 23.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 23% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 21 covering analysts target $260 on average, 13% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 6% falls short of the cost of capital of 8.9%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It runs a 56% gross margin and converts 21% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.78x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.6x equity multiplier).
It spends 6.5% of revenue on R&D and 1.2% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 3.4x net debt to EBITDA ($5.7B of cash against $18.4B of debt), with interest covered 17.7x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.5, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 52% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.9% over 3 years, 2.0% over 5 years and 1.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
At current returns, reinvesting 92% of profits supports about 5.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -0.6% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.04, a backlog worth 21% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 3%.
Capex runs 1.5x depreciation (4.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 10.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 83%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (7 sales, net $21.5M sold).
It returns 2.5% a year to shareholders (1.9% in buybacks and 0.7% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 33 consecutive years, raising it 7.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 58,000 employees, each generates about $424K of revenue, in line with the Healthcare median, and productivity has risen 5.0% a year.
That works out to $91K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.6M (6x revenue per employee).
